Most of a drone day is spent standing in a field.

This is the part nobody puts in the reel. A road through the polder, a bag of batteries in the van, and a lot of looking at the sky to see what the clouds are doing.

The shot list said golden hour. The weather said maybe. So we waited.

People think aerial work is about the drone. It is not. It is about timing. You get one window where the light is low and warm and the grass goes gold, and it lasts about forty minutes. Everything before that is preparation so you do not waste a second of it.

Batteries charged the night before. Flight path walked on foot first, so we know where the ditches are. Airspace checked. Landing spot picked. Backup landing spot picked, because the first one usually has a tractor on it by the time you need it.

Then you fly. Three takes, maybe four. Land, swap battery, fly again. The drone is up for six minutes at a time. The day is eight hours.

The Inspire 3 gives us full frame, clean low light and a gimbal that holds a slow push without wobbling. Useful, but it is still just a camera on a stick that flies. The choice of where to put it is the actual work.

So yes, this is the glamour. One person, one field, one drone, and a sky that is deciding whether to cooperate.

It did, in the end. The light came through around eight. We got what we came for.

If you are planning something that needs air, tell us early. We can build the ground schedule around the light instead of hoping for it.
